candidates.abstract: The realm of high-performance computing has expanded to include machine learning tasks of many forms. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are becoming increasingly popular, with their applications expanding across diverse domains. As the scale of graph data continues to grow, including larger numbers of nodes, edges, and higher embedding dimensions, standardized libraries such as DGL and PyG have been developed to facilitate GNN computation. These libraries allow the computation to be described a a high level of abstraction, providing high productivity on the part of the developer. However, with the rapid increase in the number of processor cores and the evolution of multicore architectures, these libraries often show poor scalability and fail to execute GNN inference efficiently on the latest multicore systems, particularly those with upwards of a hundred cores. To address this limitation, we introduce FrontGI, a fast and scalable set of techniques that advances the frontier of GNN inference on large-scale graphs (over 100,000 vertices) by leveraging graph-property- and architecture-aware design. FrontGI employs different parallelization strategies optimized for diverse graph structures, maximizing the utilization of multi-level cache hierarchies in multicore systems. We evaluate a number of GNN models with FrontGI on a 128-core AMD EPYC system. Compared to state-of-the-art libraries, FrontGI achieves up to 3.35$\times$, 3.20$\times$, 2.89$\times$ and 3.10$\times$ speedups over DGL for GCN, GraphSAGE, GIN, and SGC models, respectively, and even greater improvements over PyG, across a range of large-scale, high-dimensional graph datasets with diverse structural properties.
candidates.title: FrontGI: Architecture-Aware Parallel GNN Inference on Chiplet-Based Multicore Systems

candidates.abstract: A graph neural network (GNN) forecasting a collection of load series combines two mechanisms, sharing parameters across series and reading neighboring series, and a gain over a non-graph model may come from either; telling them apart decides whether a graph is worth maintaining. We propose a model diagnostic protocol that compares the GNN with three reference models: a per-node network, a network shared across nodes without neighbors, and the same GNN without edges. Degree-preserving rewiring tests whether neighbor identity matters. After a tuned benchmark on regional load in France and on low-voltage feeders in the UK, we apply the protocol to deliberately short node histories, as when non-stationary demand leaves only recent observations relevant: the feeders, within one week, and a public dataset of client consumption series. On the feeders, sharing parameters recovers most of the error gap between node-specific models and GNNs, about two thirds against a regularized one. Adding the edges to an otherwise identical backbone brings a smaller gain, half or more of which disappears under rewiring. On the client series, the neighbor mean degrades the per-node model on the shorter window and the edges'gain is not consistently distinguishable from zero; on the regions of France, where each node's own history is already informative, the ranking between per-node models and GNNs changes with tuning. A synthetic study points to noisy local measurements as one regime where neighbors help. In an exploratory online aggregation, graph and non-graph forecasters appear complementary, and the weight assigned to GNNs is not proportional to their contribution. In none of the three datasets do the edges account for most of a GNN's advantage over node-specific models, so a forecasting gain should be credited to the graph only after comparison with per-node and shared references.
candidates.title: A Diagnostic Protocol for GNNs in Electricity Load Forecasting: Separating Parameter Sharing from Neighborhood Access

candidates.abstract: Illicit account detection is a critical task for financial risk control systems, aiming to pinpoint malicious actors within transaction networks. Existing efforts typically recast transaction networks into directed multigraphs and leverage graph neural networks (GNNs) to detect anomalies via topological structures under the homophily assumption. However, directly grafting GNNs onto transaction graphs is faced with at least two pivotal challenges, i.e., structural inconsistency and label scarcity. The former arises from deceptive connections forged by malicious actors, while the latter stems from the lack of annotated data. In light of these, we introduce MINT, a novel graph neural framework that mitigates structural inconsistency via an attentive message-passing scheme on transaction graphs. Specifically, MINT introduces a discrepancy-aware feature propagation, which tracks malicious actors by quantifying deviations between nodes across bi-directional transaction flows. A transaction salience module is proposed to mitigate structural inconsistency by adaptively regularizing the interaction strength between nodes. Furthermore, to alleviate label scarcity, MINT is optimized via Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning, which exploits only a minority of illicit nodes coupled with a majority of unlabeled ones. Extensive experiments conducted on three financial transaction benchmarks, including two large-scale public and one in-house real-world datasets, validate the superior effectiveness of MINT over several cutting-edge baselines.
candidates.title: MINT: Mitigating Structural Inconsistency via Attentive Message Passing for Financial Anomaly Detection

candidates.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used in modern machine learning, yet most existing frameworks remain fundamentally static, limiting their applicability in Dynamic Data Driven Application Systems (DDDAS) where observations arrive sequentially under uncertainty. We introduce B-EAGLe (Bayesian Evidence Accumulation for Graph-Based Learning), a probabilistic framework inspired by CBGT-Net (cortico-basal ganglia-thalamic network) that reformulates graph classification as a sequential evidence accumulation process. B-EAGLe combines a GNN encoder with a Bayesian accumulator that incrementally updates posterior beliefs over class labels as new observations arrive, committing to a decision only when sufficient confidence is achieved. Experiments on CIFAR10 demonstrate competitive performance together with principled confidence estimation under sequential observations.
candidates.title: Bayesian Evidence Accumulation for Graph-Based Learning in Dynamic Data-Driven Applications Systems

candidates.abstract: Link prediction remains difficult in sparse graphs, where diffusion heuristics lack connectivity and geometric methods suffer spectral instability when coupling learned representations with diffusion operators. We introduce Concorde, an energy-based framework that resolves this by decomposing link likelihood into three structurally decoupled branches: (i) a parameter-free spectral anchor that establishes permutation-invariant topological stability; (ii) a mixed-curvature residual on a learnable $\mathbb{H}^{d_h}_{c_h} \times \mathbb{S}^{d_s}_{c_s}$ product manifold, regularized by a feature-aware Ollivier-Ricci curvature proxy; and (iii) a continuous vector field on the tangent bundle of hyperbolic space for non-local structural alignment across topological gaps. The branches are fused via learned gating and trained with an N-pair ranking loss aligned with retrieval-style evaluation. Across five benchmarks spanning sparse, dense, featureless, and attributed regimes, Concorde establishes state-of-the-art early retrieval precision, nearly doubling P@10% over leading baselines in sparse settings.
candidates.title: Concorde: Geometry-Aware Link Prediction via Decoupled Energy Minimization

candidates.abstract: Spatio-temporal graph neural networks combine a node's history with information from graph neighbors. The central question is whether graph neighbors provide predictive information beyond each node's own history. Forecast accuracy depends on both the choice of neighbors and the way graph messages enter the temporal model. We study these choices as graph construction and graph exposure on U.S. state unemployment, traffic speed, and electricity demand. Our diagnostic design uses two comparisons: varying exposure while holding the domain graph fixed, and varying construction while holding late gated integration fixed. A GRU using only each node's own history and randomized graph controls help assess what the graph contributes. Under a common change forecasting protocol, the same domain graph can improve or worsen error relative to the GRU across integration designs. Late integration alone is insufficient, while adding a fusion gate yields lower mean error in all three tasks. With late gated integration fixed, a graph based on residual correlations has the lowest mean error among the tested graphs, although randomized graphs perform similarly on unemployment. The findings support evaluating graph construction and integration together, with conclusions tied to the comparisons actually performed.
candidates.title: How Much Graph Is Too Much? Graph Construction and Exposure in Spatio-Temporal Forecasting

candidates.abstract: Structured scientific spectra encode rich physical information while obeying hard constraints, such as conservation laws and characteristic spectral geometry. Accurate prediction of these spectra is central to materials discovery, yet existing methods often treat them as unconstrained sequences and therefore fail to enforce the underlying physical structure. Taking electronic density of states (eDOS) as the prototypical example, we introduce DeepSciReasoner, a general paradigm for predicting scientific spectra under physical constraints. The framework combines structure-aware spectrum decoding with constraint-preserving physical reasoning, allowing predictions to capture rich spectral structure while respecting the underlying physics. We evaluate DeepSciReasoner on eDOS, phonon density of states (phDOS), X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), and Raman spectra, where it substantially improves prediction accuracy while maintaining physical consistency. These results establish DeepSciReasoner as a reusable blueprint for structured scientific spectrum prediction under hard physical constraints.
candidates.title: Deep Scientific Reasoning under Physical Constraints: Structure-Aware Spectrum Prediction

candidates.abstract: On million-node graphs, the memory wall arrives before the compute wall: a GNN that never fits in VRAM cannot deliver the all-node inference its accuracy promises. The standard remedy, pruning, has always been an accuracy tax - paid once and never refunded. DPR refuses this framing. Its central insight is that the mask that shrinks training can also scaffold recovery: one compact node set bounds both computations of graph learning, serving as the encoder's training graph and, at inference, as the anchor from which a sparse structure-aware decoder rebuilds every pruned node (double-layer sparsification). The order is inverted - prune for efficiency, then reconstruct for accuracy - and the tax is repaid: the deployed 30%-budget model trains in 1,450 MiB of peak memory on one 6 GB GPU and recovers 96.9% of its dense-reconstruction reference, beating a same-GPU rerun of the edge-sparsification baseline DSpar by +1.36 pp at 50.1% lower peak training memory; against the same-protocol full-batch no-prune encoder the deployed point pays a measured 2.64 pp accuracy tax for a 2.8x smaller training footprint. Pruning without reconstruction leaves the encoder at 0.378 within the same 40-epoch window (Fig. 4), and all-node serving runs 46x faster than sampling-based GraphSAGE, giving up approx. 5.4 pp of test accuracy. The framework scales to a 2.45M-node production graph at 6,285 MiB of peak training memory; extended variants (long-range context, external text features, a CAN-bus application) are reported as extensions and do not compete with the deployed method, and the 41.8%-budget M4 point, scored on a coarsened super-node graph with its own split, is reported separately rather than compared with the original-node baselines. DPR thus turns aggressive node pruning from an accuracy tax into a safe training accelerator for VRAM-limited all-node inference.
candidates.title: Decoupled Prune-and-Reconstruct: Training on a Compact Core with Double-Layer Sparsification

candidates.abstract: Correlated corroboration can make knowledge-based systems overconfident when dependent reports are treated as independent evidence. This paper presents an influence-aware evidence aggregation architecture that makes source dependence explicit and constrains confidence growth under partial dependence knowledge. The architecture combines an influence-indexed evidence graph (EIIG), a generalised estimate of effective independent evidence (EIE) with graded dependence weights, and a bounded confidence-propagation rule (CONFPROP). We evaluate the architecture against three baselines—naive independence aggregation, a Bayesian independence update, and a source-discounted comparator—across four controlled synthetic scenarios and a semi-realistic external case study using 500 claims from the FEVER fact-verification corpus. Under the strongest synthetic dependence regimes, CONFPROP consistently reduces confidence inflation relative to naive aggregation: inflation ratios are 4.00 in a common-parent echo-chamber scenario and 10.00 in a fully duplicated cascade, while no suppression occurs when evidence is genuinely independent. A factorial sensitivity analysis across 648 parameter combinations per stress-test scenario confirms that the discount factor γ decreases with the diversification threshold K and increases with the unknown-status weight α. The architecture provides deterministic, auditable confidence updates with structured monitoring signals, and is designed for modular integration into existing knowledge-based systems operating under uncertain source dependence.
candidates.title: Echo chamber dynamics and influence aware evidence aggregation for epistemic integrity in knowledge based systems

candidates.abstract: Graph Neural Networks are widely used to learn structural representations of relational data. Hierarchical graph pooling learns multi-level representations by progressively coarsening graphs; however, prior methods rely on predefined cluster numbers or fixed pooling ratios, limiting adaptability to individual graphs. We propose Graph-Dependent Pooling (GDPool), which dynamically determines pooling granularity for each graph. We analyze optimization conflicts among layer-wise objectives through gradient alignment, showing that independently supervised pooling levels can send conflicting gradients to shared parameters. GDPool uses self-attention to select graph-specific anchors representing structurally important nodes and constructs coarse graphs through soft node assignment. Experiments on metal-organic framework and molecular graph benchmarks show that GDPool consistently achieves the best predictive performance across all benchmarks. Evaluations using modularity and the effective number of clusters show that GDPool achieves consistently higher modularity than existing methods while the number of active clusters decreases monotonically with depth. Sensitivity analyses confirm stable behavior across hyperparameter and architectural choices.
candidates.title: Graph-dependent pooling: adaptive granularity in hierarchical graph neural networks

candidates.abstract: Before every neutral objective in professional League of Legends, each team decides which of its five players walk to the pit, which hold a lane, and when to commit. The leading analysis of such setups, TAGNet for Counter-Strike 2, clusters graph-network embeddings of player positions and reads cluster win rates as tactical quality. We treat a setup as an allocation on a walled map: formations are set partitions on the lattice $\Pi_5$, control is a geodesic Voronoi split of a navigation graph, and commitment is an allocation game solved as a quantal response equilibrium priced in win probability. On all 164 games of MSI and Worlds 2025 (2,994 team-setups, minimap tracks validated against Riot positions), trailing teams leave the pit empty far more often than leading teams, by +34.8 percentage points at the first baron and +30.4 percentage points at Atakhan. Our model, HASSE-QRE, finds six setup patterns that whole-model series-bootstrap refits reproduce (ARI 0.819, comparable to 0.813 for TAGNet's $K$-Means step alone) and indicates that teams price fights, travel and committed players, not the objective itself (weight 0.018; fixing it to one costs 59.9 log-likelihood points). The equilibrium reproduces a quarter of the commitment gap, almost all of it through state variables rather than its strategic channels. Weighting a team-level contrast by exposure moves it across $p=0.05$ (0.046 against 0.052). We release the tracks, setups and code.
candidates.title: Allocation Before the Clock: Graph, Set and Game Theory of Professional League of Legends Objective Setups

candidates.abstract: The classification of research papers from different academic data is still challenging due to the presence of semantic ambiguity, lack of information, fluctuating credibility, and complex linkages across research articles. Existing fuzzy graph neural networks depend too much on membership information and cannot truly consider the intuitionistic uncertainty, trust dependability, and structural importance of nodes at the graph propagation level. To overcome these constraints, this paper presents an intuitionistic fuzzy graph neural network architecture that combines trust-aware intuitionistic representations and a unique node Laplacian energy mechanism. The suggested Node Laplacian Energy is derived from the graph Laplacian's row-wise norm and is used as an adaptive node-weighting metric to assess each research paper's local structural contribution. Furthermore, a diffusion-based propagation technique is used to enhance information transmission across semantically linked publications and capture larger graph relationships. The suggested system is tested for research-paper categorization with semantic similarity features and intuitionistic fuzzy credibility information. Its performance is compared to known machine learning and graph neural network baselines utilizing accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. The findings show that including uncertainty-aware representations, structural node weighting, and diffusion-based graph propagation can improve discriminative academic content categorization. The suggested paradigm offers a unified way to model semantic linkages, uncertainty, believability, and graph structural relevance in research-paper categorization.
candidates.title: An energy-aware diffusion graph neural network based on intuitionistic fuzzy credibility graphs for research-paper classification

candidates.abstract: Accurate prediction of drug-target affinity (DTA) is a core technical step in high-throughput drug screening and targeted drug discovery, which directly affects the efficiency of candidate compound mining and the control of research and development costs. Traditional experimental methods are difficult to meet the requirements of high-throughput screening, while existing deep learning-based models generally suffer from bottlenecks such as shallow fusion of multi-source heterogeneous features, insufficient mining of interactive features, and inadequate generalization robustness. To address these issues, we propose HAFI-DTA (Hierarchical Attention-Guided and Feature Iterative Interaction for Multimodal Drug-Target Affinity Prediction). Specifically, our framework employs a hierarchical attention mechanism to guide the fusion of multi-source heterogeneous features, and combines a two-layer GRU with iterative interaction to capture the deep correlations among features. Experimental results on the KIBA and Davis datasets demonstrate that the proposed HAFI-DTA model achieves overall performance comparable to the current state-of-the-art, while delivering stable and modest improvements in both CI and MSE metrics. Moreover, under the most challenging drug–target double cold-start scenario, our model attains the best performance, exhibiting excellent generalization robustness. In addition, interpretability analysis shows that the model can automatically focus on the key residues of the real binding pockets of proteins, providing an important basis for subsequent drug design and binding mode research.
candidates.title: HAFI-DTA: an interpretable multimodal framework for drug-target affinity prediction based on hierarchical attention guidance and feature iterative interaction
GD-GAT: a robust dam displacement prediction framework integrating spatial priors and gated graph attention network

candidates.abstract: This study presents a novel data-driven methodology for extraction causal chains from high-dimensional climate datasets, with a particular focus on detecting and visualizing the pathways that link climate anomalies across geographically distant regions. The proposed framework is designed to be computationally efficient while maintaining high interpretability, making it suitable for large-scale analytical applications in climate science. To assess its effectiveness, the methodology is applied to the well-studied teleconnection between the El Niño—Southern Oscillation and precipitation variability in Northeastern Brazil—a region highly susceptible to climate extremes such as droughts. The approach integrates clustering method, causal inference technique, and optimized path selection algorithm to construct interpretable causal chain graphs. Results demonstrate the methodology’s strong capability to identify key causal relationships and reproduce known climate phenomena. By effectively managing complex and massive climate data, this methodology contributes to the advancement of data science tools for climate analytics and offers valuable insights for understanding global climate teleconnections.
candidates.title: A multivariate causal chain detection methodology assessed on the ENSO modulation of the Northeastern Brazil precipitation
candidates.venue: International Journal of Data Science and Analysis

candidates.abstract: Accurate probabilistic forecasting of geographically distributed photovoltaic (PV) generation is challenged by incomplete measurements, weather-dependent cross-site correlations, and quantile crossing. This study proposes a physics-guided framework that integrates a physics-informed Wasserstein generative adversarial network with gradient penalty (PIL-WGAN-GP), a dual-exploration spatiotemporal graph neural network (DEST-GNN), and an arbitrary-quantile recurrent decoder (AQ-RNN). The imputation module combines self-supervised masking, solar geometry, a clear-sky-based power envelope, and deterministic projection. The forecasting module fuses a static spatial prior with a time-varying dependency graph, while the decoder predicts aggregate PV quantiles directly through bounded positive spacings and monotone interpolation. The framework was evaluated in a retrospective case study using hourly PV generation records from 11 Belgian regional PV zones and matched meteorological records in 2025. For 3-, 6-, and 12-h consecutive gaps, PIL-WGAN-GP reduced normalized mean absolute error from 1.450%, 2.473%, and 5.252% for linear interpolation to 0.869%, 1.027%, and 1.300%, respectively. Hard projection eliminated nighttime leakage and upper-envelope violations. Across 1-, 6-, 12-, and 24-h horizons, DEST-GNN-AQ reduced the average daylight nMAE from 3.689% for the no-graph AQ-RNN to 3.509%, with the main gains occurring at 6–24 h. The model generated nested 50%, 70%, 80%, and 90% prediction intervals with a zero quantile-crossing rate. Their empirical coverages were 41.72%, 62.81%, 69.84%, and 85.26%, indicating that structural validity was achieved while calibration remains improvable. Collectively, these findings validate the proposed framework’s ability to bridge physically admissible data reconstruction with reliable, non-crossing probabilistic forecasting for PV clusters.
candidates.title: Physics-guided non-crossing probabilistic forecasting for distributed photovoltaic clusters using dynamic graph attention

candidates.abstract: This study focuses on the spatiotemporal prediction of supply chain finance risk contagion and constructs a model based on the dynamic graph attention diffusion mechanism for in-depth exploration. The risk-aware dynamic graph attention network (DyGAT) is used to model the time-varying network structure of supply chain finance, where the spatial attention weight α_ij(t) is updated adaptively at each time step by integrating real-time risk intensity signals to realize real spatiotemporal coupling modeling. A bounded diffusion mechanism with natural risk attenuation is introduced to characterize the propagation process of risks in spatial and temporal dimensions, avoiding unbounded cumulative defects in traditional formulas. Methodologically, a supply chain finance dynamic graph structure is constructed by integrating multisource data such as historical transaction data and corporate financial information, with clear data cleaning, fusion and feature engineering processes, and the model is trained, validated and ablated strictly. The results show that the model can effectively predict the spatiotemporal paths and topological characteristics of supply chain finance risk contagion and identify key nodes and critical periods of risk propagation, and the ablation experiment verifies that the dynamic attention module and bounded diffusion module bring 18.2% and 12.5% precision improvement, respectively. It provides strong support for financial institutions and supply chain enterprises to formulate risk prevention strategies in advance and is of great significance for improving the stability and resilience of the supply chain finance system. However, caution is needed when applying the model to small-sample settings, as the limited sample size may constrain its generalizability to other industries and regions.
candidates.title: Research on the spatiotemporal prediction of supply chain finance risk contagion based on a dynamic graph attention diffusion mechanism

candidates.abstract: Technology flow (TF) forecasting aims to predict whether a technology will be utilized by another, which is significant for future cross-integration technology innovation. Although existing methods have made substantial progress in intra-domain TF forecasting, inter-domain TF forecasting remains underexplored and faces several fundamental challenges. Specifically, semantic gaps between technologies from different domains hinder effective representation learning; historical inter-domain TFs are highly sparse, limiting the ability to learn reliable structural dependencies; and intra-domain and inter-domain TFs exhibit distinct flow patterns, which are difficult to model within a unified framework. To address these challenges, in this paper, we propose an LLM-enhanced Graph Contrastive Learning (LGCL) framework that supports both intra-domain and inter-domain TF forecasting. Specifically, we first leverage LLMs with bias-aware representation adjustment to generate semantically enriched and accurate technology representations to bridge gaps across multiple domains. Then, to mitigate the sparsity of inter-domain TF data, a technology co-occurrence view is incorporated to complement historical TF information. We further develop a non-negative contrastive learning module to integrate the TF and co-occurrence views, enabling effective representation alignment without relying on negative samples. In addition, we design decoupled loss functions to separately supervise intra-domain and inter-domain flows, mitigating the difficulty of jointly modeling their different flow patterns under a unified objective. Finally, experiments on real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of our approach and provide valuable insights into future technology flow trends. Our code is available at https://github.com/huijieliu2023/LGCL.
candidates.title: LLM-enhanced Graph Contrastive Learning for Technology Flow Forecasting

candidates.abstract: Graph anomaly detection (GAD) aims to identify irregular entities in graph-structured data, yet heterogeneous anomaly patterns and distributional differences across graphs challenge generalizable detection. Existing training-free approaches avoid task-specific optimization but primarily rely on predefined numerical scoring rules, leaving the semantic interpretation of heterogeneous anomaly evidence largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose Jev-GAD, a training-free generalist graph anomaly detection framework that bridges heterogeneous numerical evidence and pretrained decision mechanisms. To address heterogeneous anomaly patterns, we construct complementary structural, attribute, and neighborhood evidence and transform heterogeneous statistics into graph-relative anomaly percentiles. To move beyond predefined numerical scoring rules, we leverage a single frozen pretrained language model for evidence-conditioned anomaly assessment. To bridge the semantic gap between numerical evidence and pretrained models, we design a semantic Graph-to-State (G2S) transformation that organizes graph context and semantically labeled node evidence into structured decision states for non-generative option-logit readout. The resulting decision scores are integrated with four complementary statistical scores through equal-weight rank-based fusion, without GAD-specific gradient-based optimization. Extensive experiments on seven graph anomaly detection benchmarks spanning citation, social, and co-review networks demonstrate the effectiveness of Jev-GAD, achieving average AUROC and AUPRC scores of 89.18\% and 52.40\%, respectively. Further analyses validate the contributions of pretrained decision readout and semantic evidence grounding.
candidates.title: One Pretrained Decision Model Is Enough for Training-Free Generalist Graph Anomaly Detection
A unified, causal recommender for temporal preferences, signed influence, and diversity
GAMMA-Traffic: dynamic graph-based attention and multi-head cross-correlation for traffic congestion prediction
EGNN: A graph-based intrusion detection framework considering class-imbalanced problem
FuseNet-DTA: a hybrid deep learning model with feature fusion attention and dual parallel CNN for drug-target binding affinity prediction

candidates.abstract: Designing optimal auctions for allocating public infrastructure-such as airport slots and energy resources-is challenging due to interdependent resources and complex side-constraints. While the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) auction guarantees maximum welfare, it cannot maximize revenue or accommodate the multi-objective trade-offs inherent in public infrastructure systems. We propose a differentiable, constraint-aware framework for combinatorial auction design that enables end-to-end learning of fractionally feasible, approximately strategy-proof mechanisms. Our primary contribution is a combinatorial constraint enforcement technique that ensures fractional feasibility by construction, bypassing the need for penalty-based approximations. We introduce CAGraph, a novel graph-based architecture designed to capture dependencies between items and bidders, alongside CANet and CAFormer as deep learning baselines, for combinatorial settings. We also provide a Matching Pursuit-inspired decomposition that maps fractional allocations to feasible discrete allocations and empirically evaluates the resulting discretization gap. In synthetic benchmarks and an airport slot-divestiture case study, respectively, the learned mechanisms achieve up to 73.5% and 180% higher expected revenue than VCG, under small empirical regret. Finally, we visualize the Pareto frontiers for revenue, welfare, and fairness, providing regulators with a decision-support tool to design infrastructure auctions that balance profitability, efficiency and equity.
candidates.title: Differentiable Combinatorial Auction Design: Optimizing Revenue-Welfare-Fairness Frontiers With Graph Attention Networks

candidates.abstract:
Spatial multi‐omics technologies jointly profile multiple molecular layers in situ, enabling integrated characterization of tissue organization and cellular states. However, many graph-based approaches remain computationally demanding because they rely on repeated message passing over global graphs, whereas naive local sampling may disrupt cell-level correspondence when multimodal features and graph topologies are not induced synchronously. Moreover, simple concatenation or fixed-weight fusion does not explicitly account for unequal uncertainty between expression‐derived and spatial evidence, making the learned representations sensitive to feature corruption, technical noise and modality inconsistency.
 
 
 
 We present SubPoE, a subgraph-induced Product-of-Experts framework for spatial multi‐omics integration. SubPoE synchronously induces aligned local subgraphs from modality‐specific molecular similarity graphs and a shared spatial graph, preserving molecular‐similarity topology correspondence while reducing per‐iteration graph complexity. Dual‐topology variational graph encoders model expression-derived structure and spatial context as probabilistic experts, which are adaptively fused according to their uncertainty through a Product‐of‐Experts formulation. A composite self-supervised objective further improves robustness and cross‐modal alignment.
 
 
 
 Across eight public paired spatial multi‐omics datasets, SubPoE achieves competitive and comparatively stable performance against existing methods. Ablation, sensitivity, robustness and efficiency experiments further support the contributions of synchronous subgraph induction and uncertainty‐aware fusion.
 
 
 
 These results establish SubPoE as an effective approach for learning topology‐preserving, uncertainty-aware representations of heterogeneous spatial multi‐omics data.
candidates.title: SubPoE: a subgraph-induced Product-of-Experts framework for spatial multi-omics integration

candidates.abstract: Manufacturing operators must maintain production while limiting emissions when disturbances spread through shared resources. This simulation-only study examines that trade-off in a reduced-order, five-layer manufacturing network; no physical-plant calibration or live digital-twin connection is available. The prototype combines sparse hypergraph risk features, temporal damage memory and a soft actor-critic controller with carbon and tail-excess penalties. Trained policies are evaluated on four held-out synthetic networks using 50 paired disturbance seeds and three initialization seeds. The proposed controller achieves mean resilience 0.875, compared with 0.442 without intervention and 0.947 for HG-SAC. Its emissions are 24.0% lower than HG-SAC, but it exceeds the allowance in 87.5% of trajectories. Paired effect sizes, multiplicity corrections, retrained ablations and shifted-disturbance tests clarify the trade-offs and limitations. The results show a trade-off between emissions and resilience under the simulated conditions. Prospective plant calibration and shadow validation remain necessary.
candidates.title: Hypergraph-informed cascading risk control for low-carbon manufacturing: a simulation study for digital-twin development

candidates.abstract: Chip placement strongly affects routed wirelength and thermal behavior, yet these downstream metrics are difficult to evaluate during macro placement. Learning-based macro placers commonly optimize the macro-only half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL), denoted mHPWL, which ignores standard cell connectivity and spatial demand. In contrast, analytical mixed-size placers optimize differentiable full netlist wirelength and density objectives but are typically unaware of thermal effects. We propose EGGPlacer, an energy-guided diffusion framework that incorporates analytical placement feedback and thermal feedback into macro placement generation. An analytical placer acts as an online physical response model, exposing the standard cell distribution and a full netlist wirelength proxy induced by each intermediate macro placement, while a differentiable thermal model provides temperature feedback. These signals are formulated as composable energies and injected throughout reverse diffusion without retraining the underlying generative model. Experiments on public placement benchmarks show that EGGPlacer achieves competitive mixed-size HPWL relative to strong analytical and learning-based macro placers. In the end-to-end evaluation, EGGPlacer also obtains the lowest average routed wirelength and peak temperature among the evaluated methods. Ablation studies further demonstrate that analytical and thermal guidance provide distinct and complementary benefits across wirelength proxies, routed wirelength, and thermal objectives.
candidates.title: EGGPlacer: Energy-Guided Generative Chip Placement with Diffusion Models

candidates.abstract: Protein classifiers are highly sensitive to evaluation protocol: random train/test splits induce phylogenetic leakage, allowing models to exploit taxon-specific correlations and substantially overestimate out-of-distribution performance. This issue is particularly acute for venom compound classification by ion-channel target (Ca2+, K+, Na+), where reported accuracies of 80-90% do not reflect generalization to unseen taxa. We formulate cross-species prediction as a structured distribution shift in which taxonomic identity acts as a confounder, requiring representations that capture structural features invariant across phylogeny. Using a shared multimodal backbone that fuses ESM-2 sequence embeddings with a disulfide-aware graph attention network, we systematically compare five structural inductive biases (spectral, Riemannian, SE(3)-invariant, statistical-manifold, and persistent-homology representations) under a leave-one-taxon-out evaluation protocol on a benchmark of 1,373 ColabFold-predicted venom compounds spanning five taxa. The persistent-homology representation summarizes backbone geometry through topological descriptors that are robust to local structural perturbations, providing an inductive bias toward phylogenetically invariant learning. Under conventional i.i.d. splits, all models achieve similar accuracy (81-86%), masking differences in inductive bias. Under taxonomic shift, this parity collapses: a sequence-only baseline drops to approximately 30%, the remaining geometric priors cluster at 54-55%, while our persistent-homology model (PH-GNN) achieves 63.4%, outperforming the next-best method by over 8 percentage points. These results demonstrate that random-split evaluation obscures meaningful differences in representation quality and identify topological representations as an effective inductive bias for learning under structured biological distribution shift.
candidates.title: Escaping the Phylogenetic Trap: Persistent Homology Enables Cross-Species Ion Channel Classification via Multimodal Graph Neural Networks

candidates.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are among the standard tools for molecular property prediction, but the atom-level explanations of their predictions are hard for medicinal chemists to act on. We propose a change of input representation rather than a new model: molecules are encoded as fragment-level graphs from BRICS decomposition, where each node is a synthetically meaningful fragment whose features are the element-wise sum of its atoms'features. Because only the representation changes, any message-passing GNN and any post-hoc attribution method produces explanations at the resolution of functional groups instead of single atoms. Across four architectures, four prediction tasks, and two explainers under scaffold splits, fragment-level encoding matches atom-level test accuracy on roughly five-fold smaller graphs. Integrated-Gradients attributions recover known pharmacophores above chance on two enzyme targets, namely BACE at 1.5 times the chance rate, and PTR1 at 3.2 times. A like-for-like comparison against an aggregated atom-level baseline shows that post-hoc aggregation is not a stable substitute: its BACE hit rate range both exceeds and falls below the fragment model's hit rate depending on two arbitrary aggregation choices, whereas fragment-level training yields a single convention-free attribution at no predictive cost. The code is available at: https://github.com/4D-Lab/frame
candidates.title: Fragment-Level Graph Encoding for Interpretable Molecular Property Prediction
How Geospatial Effects Can Affect Predictive Learning: A Novel Predictability Framework Consisting of Geographic Entropy and Knowledge Graph

candidates.abstract:
Lane localization is an important component of advanced driver assistance systems and autonomous driving, where accurate estimation of lane geometry is essential for safe vehicle navigation. Nevertheless, the current lane detection algorithms may face difficulties in complex driving situations due to poor visual feature extraction, unstable temporal prediction, and inadequate modeling of structural relations between lanes.
 
 
 
 In order to overcome these issues, this paper introduces the unified spatio-temporal graph learning approach that integrates spatial feature extraction, temporal context aggregation, uncertainty-driven graph formation, graph attention reasoning, and geometric optimization. The proposed GraphLane framework dynamically learns graph connections between lane keypoints while incorporating uncertainty estimation to suppress unreliable feature interactions and temporal consistency to improve structural stability across consecutive frames. A geometry-aware optimization strategy is further introduced to encourage smooth and physically consistent lane predictions. The framework was evaluated on the CULane test set using the proposed row-anchor-based lane-existence and localization evaluation.
 
 
 
 Experimental results show that the proposed GraphLane framework achieves a lane-existence precision of 0.9769, recall of 0.8990, F1-score of 0.9363, and an average localization error of 19.28 pixels. Qualitative analysis shows that the framework produces smooth and consistent lane predictions under occlusions, shadows, dense traffic, and nighttime conditions.
 
 
 
 Other analyses on learned graphs, computational complexity, and ablation studies also show that incorporating temporal context, adaptive graph reasoning, and geometrically informed optimizations is effective for lane localization.
candidates.title: GraphLane: a spatio-temporal graph learning framework for lane localization

candidates.abstract: Approximate solutions of partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured grids can be represented on a graph. Numerical optimization involving stiff evolutionary and static PDEs often requires solving a large system of equations, which can be treated as a constraint. In this work, we present a fully differentiable graph-based implicit solver that incorporates this constraint. We evaluate its performance across four key tasks: a) linear and nonlinear forward modeling of evolutionary and static problems, b) solving inverse problems to estimate equation coefficients, c) solving inverse problems to estimate the right-hand side, and d) learnable graph coarsening to accelerate forward modeling. The stability and differentiability of our solver enable significant reductions in the complexity of forward modeling while efficiently addressing related inverse problems. These capabilities make it a powerful tool for different physics and engineering applications, in particular for geophysics, where inverse problems are commonly solved in order to reduce the model uncertainty.
candidates.title: Automatic Differentiation with Constraints in Forward and Inverse Problems

candidates.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle with temporally grounded reasoning because their static parametric memory is misaligned with the dynamic evolution of real-world knowledge. Although RAG and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) provide practical ways to enhance LLMs, they remain insufficient for temporal reasoning. Existing retrieval methods typically prioritize semantic relevance while overlooking temporal validity, event order, and evolutionary dependencies, resulting in evidence that is relevant in isolation but temporally fragmented. Meanwhile, conventional PEFT methods usually employ fixed and input-agnostic low-rank updates, making it difficult to capture time-dependent entity semantics and relation drift. To address these limitations, we propose Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment (TEPCA), a framework for LLM reasoning over TKGs. TEPCA aligns LLM reasoning with temporal knowledge at both the evidence and parameter levels. At the evidence level, it introduces time-constrained Dynamic Relevance-Guided Path (DRGP) pruning to preserve globally coherent temporal paths, together with Mutual-Information (MI)-based pruning to retain query-informative local facts under temporal constraints. At the parameter level, it integrates Dynamic-Gated LoRA (DG-LoRA), a timestamp-conditioned low-rank adaptation mechanism that dynamically modulates the effective adaptation subspace according to temporal context. This design enables LLMs to better capture fine-grained entity evolution and time-dependent relation semantics while preserving parameter efficiency. Experimental results on two TKG benchmarks demonstrate that TEPCA achieves state-of-the-art performance. Additional evaluations of DG-LoRA on eight commonsense QA datasets further verify its general input-adaptive capacity, scalability across LLM backbones, and interpretability.
candidates.title: Temporal Evidence-Parameter Co-Alignment for LLM Reasoning over Temporal Knowledge Graphs

candidates.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots require spatial representations that capture geometry and semantics while staying sparse enough for planning in large, unknown environments. Graphs provide a natural representation for this purpose and underpin both classical planning methods and a growing class of reinforcement-learning (RL) policies. However, RL training needs hundreds to thousands of parallel environments, each constructing and updating its own graph. Existing graph libraries are typically designed for either single-robot deployment or fixed graphs, and CPU-based graph construction limits scalable training to only a few dozen environments. We introduce GGraph, an open-source GPU-accelerated graph library for both robot deployment and large-scale learning. GGraph supports real robots through ROS 2 interfaces and vectorized GPU-based policy training, with built-in support for tasks including 3-D navigation, exploration, and loop-closure integration. For single-robot operation, GGraph updates graphs in milliseconds. At scale, it enables graph-based exploration policies to train across hundreds of parallel robots, reducing wall-clock training time by one order of magnitude. Across simulation and real-world experiments, these results establish GGraph as a unified graph infrastructure for both large-scale robot learning and deployment.
candidates.title: GGraph: A GPU-Accelerated Library for Graph-Based Robot Deployment and Learning

candidates.abstract: Drug combination therapy has emerged as a promising strategy for improving therapeutic efficacy. While hypergraphs have demonstrated substantial potential for high-order drug synergy modeling, existing approaches still suffer from two critical limitations: (1) reliance on locally determined aggregation limits the utilization of multihop topological context and broader structural information across the hypergraph; (2) homogeneous message passing overlooks the structural heterogeneity of drugs and cell lines within hyperedges. To address these issues, we propose GLH2Syn, a global–local dual-view heterogeneous hypergraph learning framework for drug synergy prediction. Specifically, GLH2Syn operates on a heterogeneous hypergraph in which each drug–drug–cell line triplet forms a hyperedge, incorporating two complementary views: a global diffusion view and a local topology view. The global diffusion view performs diffusion over the node–hyperedge topology to derive globally informed incidence weights, thereby incorporating structural context into local aggregation. The local topology view captures fine-grained structural heterogeneity within hyperedges through structure-aware node-hyperedge propagation, distinguishing the heterogeneous roles of drugs and cell lines in high-order interactions. Furthermore, we design a joint optimization objective integrating drug synergy prediction with similarity reconstruction to preserve both predictive accuracy and biological consistency. Extensive experiments on two public data sets demonstrate that GLH2Syn consistently outperforms 11 competitive baselines on both classification and regression tasks across three test scenarios. Case studies further validate its potential in discovering novel synergistic drug combinations.
candidates.title:
GLH2Syn: Global–Local Dual-View
Heterogeneous Hypergraph Learning for Drug Synergy Prediction
candidates.venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

candidates.abstract: Smart transportation systems produce vast amounts of dynamic graph-structured data from vehicles, roadside units, IoT sensors and V2X communication networks, posing crucial challenges related to privacy protection, adversarial resilience, explainability, and scalable federated intelligence. Current temporal graph learning systems solve these problems one at a time, leading to fragile solutions that fail in face of a real-world mix of threats. It is proposed that a unified Federated Explainable Adversarially Robust Differentially Private Temporal Graph Autoencoder (FEAR-DPTGAE) is a Federated Explainable Adversarially Robust Differentially Private Graph Autoencoder with four novel mechanisms: Federated Explainable Adversarially Robust Differentially Private Temporal Graph Autoencoder - Adaptive Temporal Graph Privacy Allocator (ATGPA): An entropy-guided framework on budget allocation per node, Federated Explainable Adversarially Robust Differentially Private Temporal Graph Autoencoder - Cross-Client Adversarial Robustness Aggregation (CARA): A protocol for Byzantine-resilient federated training, Federated Explainable Adversarially Robust Differentially Private Temporal Graph Autoencoder - Graph Attention Explainability Regularizer (GAER): A regularizer to provide consistent node attribution under privacy noise for semantically consistent graph, Federated Explainable Adversarially Robust Differentially Private Temporal Graph Autoencoder - minimax-optimal adversarial temporal graph training objective. Formal (ε,δ)-DP composition proofs are given. The evaluations on METR-LA, PEMS-BAY, VeReMi, and TDrive datasets show that FEAR-DPTGAE achieves a high anomaly detection accuracy of 96.1% at ε=1.0 with a low traffic prediction MAE of 2.14 km/h, outperforming all baselines and maintaining high Explainability Score (0.92) while being robust against up to 30% malicious clients.
candidates.title: FEAR-DPTGAE: Federated Explainable Adversarially Robust Differentially Private Temporal Graph Autoencoder for Secure Smart Transportation
candidates.venue: International Journal of Data Processing & Networking

candidates.abstract: Multi-hop question answering (QA) requires models to chain intermediate conclusions while remaining cost-aware. Existing training-free self-reflective protocols (generate ->critique ->revise) improve accuracy but operate on a flat token stream: revisions cannot identify which prior step is unreliable, and early stopping cannot exploit structural convergence. We introduce GraphEvoResearcher, a training-free protocol that lifts EvoResearcher's self-reflective meta-reward onto an explicit reasoning graph - nodes are intermediate conclusions/evidence and edges encode support, contradict, and depends_on. A graph-aware meta-reward combines correctness, efficiency, reflection, diversity, and four structural signals (connectivity, acyclicity, branch coverage, path convergence) to decide whether to revise, backtrack, or stop. A graph-convergence early-stop terminates when evidence branches converge on a single conclusion. On a real LLM (DeepSeek), over GSM8K, MATH, and BBH (n=50 each), GraphEvoResearcher reaches 98%, 92%, and 82% respectively, the highest of all baselines, with the largest gains on the hardest set (MATH: +24 pp over single-shot, +12 pp over flat reflection), while keeping construction cost bounded at ~2 steps / 4.5-5 nodes. Our results indicate the structural signal of a reasoning graph is most valuable exactly where single-step reasoning is unreliable.
candidates.title: GraphEvoResearcher: Graph-Aware Training-Free Self-Reflective Reasoning for Cost-Bounded Multi-Hop Question Answering

candidates.abstract: Second-order cone programs (SOCPs) are a fundamental class of convex optimization problems widely applied across engineering domains. Classical interior-point methods are robust and accurate, but their iterative nature can be costly in real-time or repeated-solve settings. This has motivated learning-based solvers that approximate optimizer solutions with neural networks. Recent work has increasingly studied graph neural networks (GNNs) for linear, quadratic, and second-order cone optimization, leveraging their ability to model sparse relational structure among variables, constraints, and objective functions. Most existing GNN-based solvers compress the optimization process into a single forward pass, predicting the optimizer directly without using the intermediate trajectory produced by classical solvers. We introduce SOCPNet, a recursive GNN framework that uses solver trajectories to learn an iterative SOCP solution procedure. A shared GNN model is applied repeatedly, refining the current iterate at each step and enabling inference for a variable number of iterations. Rather than predicting the solution in a single pass, SOCPNet learns from intermediate iterates to progressively refine its estimates using a trajectory-regularized training procedure. We evaluate SOCPNet on multiple datasets spanning standard SOCP problem classes and show that it consistently reduces the final solution error relative to a SOCP-GNN baseline. Finally, we demonstrate how trained SOCPNet models can be used in a hybrid optimization pipeline by warm-starting a classical interior-point solver, reducing solver iterations without loss of accuracy.
candidates.title: Learning SOCP Solver Dynamics with Graph Neural Networks

candidates.abstract: Online 3D bin packing with a bounded buffer requires irreversible item-selection and placement decisions under limited knowledge of future arrivals. Feasibility alone is insufficient, as feasible actions can produce different residual-space structures and subsequent packing opportunities. A central architectural question is how to allocate spatial reasoning between item selection and placement evaluation. We propose Spatial Affordance Retrieval (SAR), a novel learning-based framework that coordinates global item-space matching with geometry-aware placement ranking. A voxel-token spatial encoder represents 3D container occupancy, enabling a picker to match buffered items to the residual space without requiring item-specific placement proposals as inputs. After item selection, a loader ranks feasible rotation-position candidates using candidate geometry, local geometric features (LGF), and inter-candidate comparison, without directly accessing global spatial tokens. The feasible candidate set connects the two stages, which are jointly optimized under a shared long-horizon packing return. On the Random, JD, and SF datasets, the best SAR variants improve utilization over the strongest evaluated online baselines by 0.96-4.20 percentage points under the no-buffer setting (K=1). With a buffer (K=5), the best utilization rates across SAR variants reach 93.55%, 91.04%, and 90.41%, respectively. Ablations support the complementary roles of global item-space matching and geometry-aware placement evaluation, counterfactual analysis suggests that learned item selection favors greater future packing potential, and experiments demonstrate compatibility with multiple candidate generators.
candidates.title: SAR: Learning Global Item-Space Matching and Geometry-Aware Placement Ranking for Buffered Online 3D Bin Packing

candidates.abstract: EEG-eye movement emotion recognition can support mental-health monitoring and adaptive interfaces, but most fusion models treat the two signals as parallel features, classify each window alone and degrade when eye data are lost. We propose the Context-Aware Topological Distillation Graph Network (CTD-GNet), in which EEG features form the nodes of an electrode graph, and eye movements and preceding windows modulate its edges, nodes and readout, the edges through electrode-specific prompts. Bidirectional distillation of the graph, node relations and predictions couples this multimodal teacher with a single-window EEG student, improving the teacher and aligning the two graphs 35-fold. In leave-one-subject-out tests on SEED and SEED-IV against 17 baselines, CTD-GNet has the highest mean accuracy, 84.91% and 76.17%, significantly above 9 and 6 of 13 eye-based baselines after Holm correction, the smallest cross-subject spread among multimodal models and the highest worst-subject accuracy. It is the most accurate model at every rate of missing eye data on SEED-IV, keeps 66.1% on SEED without eye data, more than any EEG-only model, and stays 9.3 and 11.9 points above all single-window fusion models under eye-movement noise of one standard deviation. On film clips unseen in training, it leads on SEED with 77.1%.
candidates.title: Context-Aware Topological Distillation Graph Network for Asymmetric EEG-Eye Movement Emotion Recognition

candidates.abstract: Credit card fraud is a significant problem for financial institutions, resulting in substantial monetary loss each year. Fraud patterns and methods are continuously evolving, with fraudulent transactions often disguised to resemble legitimate activity. Real world transaction data for fraud detection is severely affected by class imbalance making it harder to detect these transactions. Fraudulent transactions are rarely isolated. Accounts, devices, and other common attributes are often shared across fraudulent activity, revealing relational patterns that individual transaction features alone cannot capture. Graph-based approaches model these relationships explicitly. However, standard graph neural networks aggregate neighbourhood information uniformly, which can dilute the already scarce signal carried by fraudulent transactions and limit detection of camouflaged fraud. This work presents RGH-GNN, a heterogeneous graph neural network that addresses this limitation by incorporating transaction-level risk scores, generated by a supervised LightGBM classifier as edge weights. It is used to guide message passing through a learnable risk-gated aggregation mechanism. It ensures that high-risk transactions contribute more strongly to learned representations rather than being diluted by uniform neighbourhood aggregation. RGH-GNN is evaluated on the IEEE-CIS fraud detection dataset against standard graph neural network models that are trained on the same heterogeneous graph. RGH-GNN outperforms all baselines across every evaluation metric, with an AUC-ROC score of 0.914. This demonstrates that incorporating engineered risk signals into graph-based message passing substantially improves fraud detection performance.
candidates.title: RGH-GNN : Risk-Gated Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network for Financial Fraud Detection

candidates.abstract: Multimodal survival prediction jointly analyzes histopathological whole-slide images (WSIs), genomic profiles, and clinical variables to stratify patients by risk. However, existing approaches often inadequately account for granularity differences across modalities, particularly in spatial organization and feature dimensionality. Within pathology, aggregating WSI patch features without preserving their spatial arrangement can obscure tissue architecture; across modalities, directly concatenating low-dimensional clinical variables with high-dimensional visual and genomic features may limit the contribution of clinical information to prediction. To address these challenges, we propose HGASurv, which introduces a hierarchical WSI encoding module and a clinical-guided graph propagation module for granularity-aware multimodal integration. The hierarchical WSI encoding module maps WSI patch features onto a spatial grid using their original coordinates and applies parallel convolutions to construct representations at patch, local-neighborhood, and regional scales. Genomic signature embeddings then query these scale-specific WSI representations through cross-modal co-attention, producing signature-conditioned morphological features. The clinical-guided graph propagation module uses clinical variables to define patient-similarity edges and propagates fused image-genomic node embeddings with graph attention, integrating clinical information through topology rather than feature concatenation. Across three TCGA cohorts, HGASurv achieved the strongest overall C-index performance, with ablation studies supporting the complementary contributions of the hierarchical WSI encoding and clinical-guided graph propagation modules. This design shows that matching representation and integration mechanisms to modality-specific granularity improves multimodal survival prediction.
candidates.title: HGASurv: Hierarchical Granularity-Aware Multimodal Integration for Survival Prediction

candidates.abstract:
Discrete interval state reconstruction of wellbore trajectory dynamics and downhole geomechanical conditions is essential for mitigating non-productive time (NPT) and optimising the rate of penetration (ROP). Conventional automated monitoring relies on empirical geomechanical formulas that fail to capture non-linear dynamics, or on supervised learning paradigms requiring manually labelled drilling dysfunction datasets, which are scarce and prone to human bias. This study introduces a Domain-informed, unsupervised hybrid deep learning architecture that couples multi-head self-attention mechanisms with spatial-cosine Graph Attention Networks (GATs) to model unlabelled logging-while-drilling (LWD) and mechanical data. Evaluated on a 205-sample directional dataset spanning 1,500 m to 6,600 m measured depth, achieving a true 24.88 m spatial resolution across 16 primary and Domain-informed variables, the proposed Hybrid Transformer GAT Autoencoder, comprising an ultra-lightweight total of 4,316 trainable parameters, was validated using a 5-fold spatially stratified Group-K-Fold protocol. The hybrid architecture achieved a reconstruction coefficient of determination (
 
 
 
 
 R
 2
 
 
 
 
 ) of 0.8895 and a mean squared error (MSE) of 0.0911, outperforming the standalone Transformer (
 
 
 
 
 R
 2

 0.8328
 
 
 
 ) and GAT (
 
 
 
 
 R
 2
 
 =
 0.5128
 
 
 
 ) baselines. Monte Carlo stochastic perturbation tests confirmed that the hybrid model retained superior noise resilience under sensor perturbations of up to 20%. Permutation feature attribution identified formation resistivity, well inclination, and an acoustic impedance proxy as the most influential variables for reconstruction performance. The proposed framework provides a compact unsupervised methodology for macro-scale interval-state reconstruction and potential future operational monitoring.
candidates.title: Unsupervised geomechanical state reconstruction in deviated wellbore using a hybrid Transformer graph attention deep learning architecture

candidates.abstract: Reliable population-graph evaluation requires separating cohort-conditioned discrimination from performance at an unseen site. We evaluate a recovered site-aware graph neural network in ABIDE-I (871 participants, 20 sites), distinguishing archived intervention results from newly recomputed controls. Archived cohort AUC was approximately 0.94, with high discrimination retained by site-only connectivity. A reconstructed ten-fold empirical site-prior classifier achieved pooled out-of-fold AUC 0.506 (95% site-resampling interval [0.418, 0.546]); simple site proportions therefore did not reproduce the high cohort result. In a budget-matched support-location experiment, the across-site mean AUC difference was +0.252 [0.184, 0.322] with directed edges but −0.003 [−0.020, 0.015] after symmetrisation, demonstrating implementation sensitivity rather than a stable support-location advantage. A supplementary leave-one-site-out analysis compared scoring-time population-edge access after the same source-site training procedure. Mean site-macro AUC was 0.577 with access and 0.580 without it; the paired difference was −0.0037 [−0.0179, 0.0111]. These observations do not establish equivalence or a complete mechanism. Explicit access contracts, compatible estimators and run-level provenance are necessary to interpret high transductive cohort performance.
candidates.title: Reliable Evaluation of Transductive Population Graph Neural Networks for Multisite Autism fMRI

candidates.abstract: ABSTRACT The growing prevalence and complexity of multimorbidity pose significant challenges to healthcare systems worldwide. Here, we developed a heterogeneous graph neural network framework for multilabel multimorbidity prediction. The framework jointly encodes symptom and diagnostic information within a heterogeneous graph and incorporates biomedical knowledge subgraphs on both the disease and symptom sides. By integrating macro‐level clinical representations of symptoms and diseases with micro‐level molecular knowledge, the model generates multilabel probabilities across candidate disease categories. We evaluated the framework in two complementary tasks: Patient‐Level Symptom–Disease Association (Task 1) and Visit‐Level Multimorbidity Completion (Task 2). In Task 1, symptoms recorded across all eligible visits within each patient's observation window were aggregated into a patient‐level symptom set to predict the disease categories recorded for that patient within the same observation window. In Task 2, symptoms and a subset of recorded positive diagnoses from the same visit were used to predict the remaining disease categories recorded for that visit. Together, these two tasks provide a unified framework for patient‐level symptom–disease association and visit‐level multimorbidity completion. The framework characterized symptom–disease–biomedical knowledge associations and non‐random patterns of disease co‐occurrence, while supporting both patient‐level symptom–disease association and visit‐level multimorbidity completion.
candidates.title: Symptom‐Driven Prediction of Chronic Multimorbidity with a Macro–Micro Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network
GLCN: a hybrid graph convolution and lite capsule network for robust and interpretable link prediction in complex networks
MO-UDRL-H: hybrid Pareto-safe distributional reinforcement learning for multi-objective cloud task allocation

candidates.abstract: Active distribution planning requires day-ahead identification of buses exposed to voltage and loading stress. Separating injection forecasting from feeder simulation leaves the contribution of multimodal fusion to node-risk estimation unresolved. We develop OSTMF-Net, an operation-state-gated topology-aware multimodal fusion network that combines temporal and graph experts through convex, residual and direct heads selected on a chronological validation holdout. Public load and NASA POWER weather variables are mapped to the IEEE 123-node OpenDSS feeder. Quasi-static time-series simulations generate deterministic 24-h absolute-risk and positive-increment targets under base, high-photovoltaic, heavy-load and combined-stress conditions. Evaluation measures agreement with OpenDSS-derived risk surrogates within this reproducible simulation benchmark. Among matched fusion methods across eight correlated scenario-target cases, OSTMF-Net obtains the lowest root mean square error (RMSE) in six and remains within 1% of the lowest value in seven. Mean case-wise RMSE reductions are 9.77%, 17.37% and 3.72% relative to a validation-selected expert, uniform averaging and linear stacking, respectively; gains over stacking concentrate in absolute-risk cases. A matched state-adaptive control yields mean RMSE 0.03460 versus 0.03080 for OSTMF-Net. Forecast perturbations, sensor-input corruption and label sensitivity assess robustness to input and target changes. On a disjoint 2013 chronology on the same feeder, OSTMF-Net records RMSE 0.03067, high-risk F1 0.795 and Top-10 agreement 1.000. The results connect complementary temporal and topology information with state-dependent correction, supporting auditable day-ahead bus-risk screening on the evaluated OpenDSS benchmark.
candidates.title: Operation state gated topology aware multimodal fusion for simulation based active distribution network risk assessment

candidates.abstract: While hierarchical structures are intrinsic to organizing human knowledge, current representation learning on text-attributed graphs predominantly operates on flat semantic spaces, overlooking the rich coarse-to-fine granularity inherent in real-world data. To bridge this gap, we propose SHiFT, which synergizes the reasoning power of LLMs with the structural representation capability of GNNs within an Expectation-Maximization (EM) paradigm. In the E-step, we harness LLMs as expert taxonomists to induce an explicit semantic tree, introducing a lightweight Mapping&Diagnosis strategy that reduces inference costs by surgically updating the hierarchy only when anomalies are detected. In the M-step, we align the GNN encoder with this induced hierarchy from complementary perspectives, including clustering partition, topological skeleton, and semantic concepts. Theoretical analysis interprets SHiFT as a generalized Variational EM algorithm. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SHiFT not only achieves state-of-the-art performance but also uncovers high-quality, human-readable taxonomies. Our code can be found at https://github.com/Cloudy1225/SHiFT.
candidates.title: Uncovering Semantic Hierarchies in Text-Attributed Graphs via Variational EM-based LLM-GNN Synergy
MGCLSyn: multimodal graph contrastive learning for drug synergy prediction

candidates.abstract: Integrating single-cell transcriptomic datasets across laboratories, conditions, and technologies remains challenging because of cell type–specific batch effects and heterogeneous biological compositions. Current methods often fail to separate genuine biological variation from technical noise, misaligning distinct cell populations or leaving batch effects uncorrected. To address these challenges, we present CellDiffusion, an unsupervised graph-based model that propagates cellular features through a diffusion process to strengthen meaningful cell-cell associations in data integration. By learning a cell-cell attention network, CellDiffusion adaptively identifies corresponding populations across batches. Our approach applies cell-specific correction in data integration, generating cell embeddings that align cells across batches while preserving intrinsic cell types and developmental trajectories. We validate CellDiffusion across various datasets, including the human endometrium, one of the most dynamic and complex tissues featuring extensive cellular and molecular changes with the menstrual cycle. This framework also improves other essential analyses such as label transfer, clustering, and trajectory inference. CellDiffusion represents a powerful paradigm for accurate single-cell transcriptomic integrative analysis.
candidates.title: CellDiffusion: Enhancing scRNA-seq data integration with accurate inference of cell-cell association

candidates.abstract: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) exploits relationships among evidence to support multi-hop question answering. However, conveying retrieved graphs through non-unique linear textual contexts to Large Language Models (LLMs) leads to graph-structure degradation and inefficient KV-cache reuse. Meanwhile, graph-structure order optimization is already NP-hard, and the additional KV-cache reuse objective further complicates the search by introducing potentially conflicting orders. To tackle these issues, we propose FuseRAG, a cost-efficient graph-based RAG framework that shifts most retrieved evidence from explicit textual contexts to latent representations. Our main idea is to separate reusable evidence content from query-aware structural interactions in latent space, while retaining only a few explicit facts as semantic anchors. The resulting latent representations are injected into decoder self-attention, where they reshape attention over evidence and thereby influence hidden states and next-token probabilities. This design preserves graph structure through latent interactions, enables evidence reuse beyond exact token-prefix matching. Experiments on three multi-hop question-answering datasets with Llama-3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B show that FuseRAG improves answer quality while achieving up to 2.7x and 2.2x TTFT speedups over the fastest graph-based baseline, respectively.
candidates.title: FuseRAG: Fusing Structure and Evidence into Inference for Cost-Efficient Graph-based RAG

candidates.abstract: Object detection in sports videos holds significant application value in tactical analysis, athlete tracking, and intelligent broadcasting. However, existing methods face two key challenges when processing sports scenes: on one hand, target distribution in sports footage is strictly constrained by field boundaries, yet generic detectors uniformly allocate detection resources across the entire image, causing frequent false detections in off-field regions due to the visual similarity between spectators and athletes; on the other hand, objects such as athletes, balls, and referees in sports scenes form stable spatial co-occurrence patterns governed by game rules, yet existing methods predict each object independently, failing to leverage cross-category relational cues to assist the detection of difficult targets. To address these issues, this paper proposes SportRGDET (Sport Relation-Graph DEtection Transformer), a framework that achieves accurate detection through two core modules: the Scene Prior Guided Module (SPGM) jointly estimates the spatial probability distribution and boundary gradient map of the field region from multi-scale encoder features, fuses them to generate a hierarchical field confidence mask, and performs spatial modulation on the deformable self-attention weights of the encoder, which reallocates attention resources toward the effective field area and progressively suppresses off-field interference across layers, thereby reducing false detections while incurring only moderate additional computation; the Relation Reasoning Enhancement Module (RREM) treats each candidate object as a node during the detection decoding stage, adaptively learns inter-node association strengths through a relation encoder based on category embeddings and relative spatial positions of node pairs, constructs a dynamic relation graph, and bidirectionally propagates contextual information across nodes via graph attention mechanisms, enabling difficult targets to refine their predictions by leveraging positional and categorical cues from surrounding identified objects, enhancing detection robustness under occlusion and blur conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that SportRGDET achieves significant performance improvements on multiple sports detection benchmark datasets, validating the effectiveness of scene prior and relation reasoning mechanisms in sports scene object detection.
candidates.title: SportRGDET: Scene prior and relation graph enhanced detection transformer for sports scenes

candidates.abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have demonstrated exceptional performance on graph-structured data. However, their success heavily relies on the availability of clean labels, an assumption that often fails in real-world scenarios. The learnability of GCNs is intrinsically linked to the neighborhood structure of nodes, making it critical to understand how this structure changes in the presence of label noise. In this work, we investigate how the neighborhood label distribution of a node changes under label noise. We mathematically derive that label noise smooths this distribution, which inherently increases its entropy and severely decreases interclass distinguishability. To address this challenge, we propose Leave-one-out Entropy Node Screening (LENS), an end-to-end framework that identifies noisy nodes by measuring the reduction in neighborhood entropy when a specific node is removed. LENS further incorporates a relabeling mechanism to recover and preserve valuable feature information instead of entirely discarding the identified noisy nodes. Crucially, the end-to-end computational overhead of LENS is remarkably low. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our algorithm achieves state-of-the-art node classification accuracy while executing an order of magnitude faster than existing noise-robust approaches.
candidates.title: A Label Noise Robust Algorithm for Graph Data using Neighborhood Label Distribution

candidates.abstract: Tissue graphs represent histology images as graphs over tissue-conforming superpixels, which keeps homogeneous tissue regions intact instead of cutting them into rectangular patches. To embed superpixels, current encoders crop them to bounding boxes and then pad, resize, or mask them, so background or fill values can leak into the node features. This matters in practice, and especially in medical imaging, where a prediction should depend on the tissue and not on an arbitrary preprocessing choice: on BACH, changing only the fill of the masked region shifts the accuracy of frozen encoders by up to 6 percentage points, larger than the differences among the four best encoders under mean fill, and the preferred fill differs between datasets, so it cannot be fixed once and for all. We present TAN (Tissue-Aware Network), a compact convolutional encoder (0.41M parameters) that processes each superpixel at its native shape and extent and excludes background from every operation, which makes its embeddings exactly invariant to the fill by construction. Under identical masks and an identical graph classifier, TAN's accuracy on BACH is not significantly different from that of the 303M-parameter foundation model UNI (81.1% vs. 80.7-82.6%, depending on the fill), with ~740x fewer parameters, ~1,190x fewer FLOPs, and no pretraining. On BRACS, TAN is close to a ResNet18 trained under the same protocol and trails the histopathology foundation models. An ablation with TAN's architecture but standard processing of fill-padded crops shows that masking keeps accuracy similar (nominally higher on BACH, lower on BRACS, within noise) at less than half the FLOPs.
